nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae drifting in the bay. They use sunlight and dissolved nutrients and feed the plankton, oysters and fish that fill the water.

nodes.name: Mangroves
nodes.desc: Salt-tolerant trees of tidal flats around the islands. Wikipedia notes that tourism development has cleared mangroves in the bay.

nodes.name: Dwarf eelgrass
nodes.desc: A seagrass recorded in GBIF near the bay. Seagrass beds shelter young fish and feed grazers, and have been lost to jetty building.

nodes.name: Karst forest trees
nodes.desc: Leafy trees and shrubs that cling to the limestone slopes of the islands, forming the moist forest on which the langurs depend.

nodes.name: Zooplankton
nodes.desc: Small drifting animals, mostly copepods, that graze phytoplankton and are in turn eaten by corals, anchovies and larval fish.

nodes.name: Oysters
nodes.desc: Filter-feeding molluscs. Wikipedia lists oysters among the shellfish of the bay, and they strain phytoplankton from the water.

nodes.name: Reef corals
nodes.desc: The Cat Ba archipelago has about 178 coral species. Reefs in deeper waters are reported to be declining from pollution.

nodes.name: Rabbitfish
nodes.desc: Plant-eating reef fish that graze seagrass and algae. They are a typical link from seagrass beds to larger fish.

nodes.name: Cat Ba langur
nodes.desc: A critically endangered primate found only on Cat Ba Island. Over 70% of its diet is leaves, and it can drink salt water.

nodes.name: Rhesus macaque
nodes.desc: The most-recorded monkey in GBIF near the bay. A flexible omnivore that eats fruit and leaves of island forests.

nodes.name: Anchovies
nodes.desc: Small schooling fish that feed on zooplankton in the open bay and are food for larger fish, seabirds and porpoises.

nodes.name: Cuttlefish
nodes.desc: Wikipedia lists cuttlefish among the bay species. They hunt small fish and crustaceans.

nodes.name: Spiny lobsters
nodes.desc: Crustaceans listed in the bay, which eat molluscs and other bottom animals and hide in rocky crevices.

nodes.name: Pacific reef heron
nodes.desc: The second most-recorded bird near the bay. It wades along rocky shores and eats small fish and crustaceans.

nodes.name: Black kite
nodes.desc: The most-recorded bird near the bay, a raptor that takes live prey and scavenges dead fish and scraps near boats and harbours.

nodes.name: Orange-spotted grouper
nodes.desc: A large reef predator of the region. It eats fish, crustaceans and cephalopods, and is a target of fishing in the bay.

nodes.name: Finless porpoise
nodes.desc: A small coastal porpoise recorded near the bay. It eats whatever is available, such as fish, crustaceans and cephalopods; gill nets are a main threat.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Warm tropical light drives the algae, seagrass and forest growth that start the web.

nodes.name: Seawater and nutrients
nodes.desc: Salty, nutrient-bearing water of the bay and its tidal flats, which feeds plankton and mangroves. Pollution and silt cloud it.

nodes.name: Rainfall
nodes.desc: Cat Ba has no rivers, streams or permanent ponds, so the forest and langurs rely on rain collected on rock and plants.

nodes.name: Limestone karst
nodes.desc: The drowned limestone towers and islets that give the bay its shape. Thin soils and caves shelter plants and animals.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Bacteria and fungi break down dead plants and animals on land and in the sea, returning nutrients.
